acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
A hydrogen nucleus is about $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$ across and light travels at about $10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (order of magnitude).

Time $\approx \dfrac{10^{-15}}{10^{8}} = 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Far too long: light covers tens of metres in $10^{-7}$ s.
perOption.B: This is the size of the nucleus in metres, not the crossing time.
perOption.C: Uses the size of a whole atom (~$10^{-10}$ m) instead of the nucleus.
perOption.D: Correct. Nuclear diameter divided by the speed of light.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
For equilibrium, the resultant torque about the support must be zero.

Since the body is balanced on a single support, the line of action of its weight must pass through the support.

perOption.A: Equal masses on each side do not give zero torque for a non-uniform body; moments depend on distances too.
perOption.B: For a non-uniform body the centre of gravity need not be at the geometric centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight then has zero moment about the support.
perOption.D: The force by the body on the support and the support's reaction are a Newton's third law pair acting on different bodies; they don't explain the body's equilibrium.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
By symmetry, the tension $T$ in both strings is the same.

The vertical components balance the weight: $2T\sin\theta = W$, where $\theta$ is the small angle each string makes with the horizontal.

Since the strings are almost horizontal, $\sin\theta$ is very small, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$ must be greater than $W$.

perOption.A: $T$ can never be less than $W/2$; two strings must at least share the weight.
perOption.B: Only true if both strings were vertical.
perOption.C: Would need $\theta \ge 30^\circ$; nearly horizontal strings give much larger tension.
perOption.D: Correct. Small $\sin\theta$ makes $T \gg W$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
By conservation of energy, loss in GPE = gain in elastic potential energy:

$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgh}{k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.22)(9.81)(0.40)}{350}} = 7.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This is $x^2$: forgets to take the square root.
perOption.B: About what you get with $h = 0.40$ cm taken as $0.004$ m (factor-of-100 error in $h$).
perOption.C: Omits $g$ from $mgh$.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
As air resistance is negligible, the acceleration ($g$) does not depend on mass, so it does not change.

The time of flight remains the same, and with the same horizontal velocity, the horizontal displacement also remains the same.

perOption.A: Correct. Motion is independent of mass without air resistance.
perOption.B: Horizontal velocity and time are unchanged, so the distance cannot decrease.
perOption.C: A heavier ball does not fall faster; vertical acceleration is $g$ for all masses.
perOption.D: Assumes heavier objects fall faster; both time and distance are unchanged.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
For vertical equilibrium, $F_y = mg$. For horizontal motion, $F_x = ma = 0.50\,mg$.

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.50mg)^2 + (mg)^2} = 1.1\,mg$.

perOption.A: Only the horizontal component $F_x$; ignores supporting the weight.
perOption.B: Only the vertical component $F_y$; ignores the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. Vector sum of the two perpendicular components.
perOption.D: Adds the components as scalars instead of as vectors.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
$a_c = r\omega^2 = r\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$.

With $T$ unchanged, $a_c \propto r$, so doubling $r$ gives $a_{\text{new}} = 2a_c$.

perOption.A: Treats $a = v^2/r$ as $\propto v^2$ only, forgetting that $r$ also doubles in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $a = v^2/r$ with $v$ held constant, but $v = 2\pi r/T$ doubles.
perOption.D: Ignores the dependence on $r$ at fixed period.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ and $M = \rho\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right)$, so $g = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$.

With the same density, $g \propto R$, so $g_A : g_B = 2 : 1$.

perOption.A: Uses $g \propto 1/R^2$ with the same mass, but the mass is not the same.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the mass ratio ($M \propto R^3$) and forgets the $1/R^2$ factor.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Total energy in orbit is $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, so

$\Delta TE = -\dfrac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(690)}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Or: $\Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(690)[(7.5\times10^{3})^2 - (7.9\times10^{3})^2] = -2.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta GPE = -GMm\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +4.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$, giving $\Delta TE = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The satellite gains total energy moving to a higher orbit.
perOption.B: This is only the gain in GPE; it ignores the loss of KE.
perOption.C: This is only the change in KE; the GPE gain is larger.
perOption.D: Treats both the KE and GPE changes as losses ($-2.1 - 4.1 \approx -6\times10^{9}$ J).

perOption.A: Uses $\omega = f$ instead of $\omega = 2\pi f$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.D: Uses an amplitude of 5.0 cm instead of 5.0 mm.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The cork vibrates with maximum amplitude at resonance, when the wave period equals the cork's natural period, $T = 0.12$ s.

$v = \sqrt{gd} = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$, so $\lambda = T\sqrt{gd} = 0.12\sqrt{9.81\times0.30} = 0.206\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.21\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Resonance: wave period equals the natural period.
perOption.D: Forgets the square root: $Tgd \approx 0.35$ m.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so twice the intensity means the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}$ times larger.

Half the frequency means the period is doubled, so the graph shows half as many cycles.

perOption.A: Doubles the amplitude, as if intensity were proportional to amplitude.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitude $\times\sqrt{2}$ and period doubled.
perOption.C: Doubles the amplitude and doubles the frequency instead of halving it.
perOption.D: Correct amplitude, but the frequency is doubled instead of halved.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The first polariser transmits half of the unpolarised light: $\tfrac{1}{2}I_0$.

By Malus' law, $I = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}I_0\right)\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{8}I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies $\cos^2 60^\circ$ but forgets the first polariser halves unpolarised light.
perOption.C: Uses $\sin^2 60^\circ$ instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ$.
perOption.D: Ignores the effect of the second polariser.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$. Since the slit-screen distance $D$ is much greater than the slit width, the angle is small.

$\theta = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}x}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so $x = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

New width: $x' = \dfrac{2(2\lambda)D}{b/2} = \dfrac{8\lambda D}{b} = 4x$.

perOption.A: Wrong proportionality; $x \propto \lambda/b$, so both changes widen the pattern.
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel, but doubling λ and halving b both increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
$\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{(1)\lambda}{d}$ and $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{(2)\lambda}{d}$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

The rate of increase of $\sin\theta$ decreases as $\theta$ increases from 0 to 90°, so $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$.

At higher orders, since the distance travelled by the light increases, intensity decreases, so the second order is dimmer.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$, but it is $\sin\theta$ that is proportional to $n$; also intensity is not the same.
perOption.B: Assumes $\theta \propto n$; it is $\sin\theta$ that doubles.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but higher orders are dimmer.
perOption.D: Correct.

perOption.C: Correct.

When a molecule collides elastically with a wall, its velocity reverses, so the magnitude of its change in momentum is twice its momentum before the collision. This change is not negligible; it is what produces the pressure.

So D is not a valid assumption.

perOption.A: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.B: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.C: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.

Movement along an equipotential surface involves zero work done, so only the radial parts of each path matter.

Paths Y and Z both end on the same (middle) equipotential, so $W_Y = W_Z$. Path X ends on the inner equipotential, closer to Q, so $W_X$ is larger.

perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Path X ends at a higher potential than Y and Z, so more work is needed.

perOption.A: $V/D$ is not the field; field depends on the gradient of $V$, not the ratio.
perOption.B: Still uses the ratio $V/D$ rather than the gradient.

perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: Current is $I=dQ/dt$. In the first three hours, $Q=(0.60)(3\times60\times60)=6480\ \mathrm{C}$. In the fourth hour the mean current is half the initial current, giving $Q=\tfrac12(0.60)(60\times60)=1080\ \mathrm{C}$. The total is $6480+1080\approx7.6\times10^3\ \mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Uses a time scale of minutes without converting it to seconds.
perOption.B: Uses the fourth-hour mean current for all four hours.

The series resistor has three times that resistance, so its potential difference is $3\times3.0=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The battery e.m.f. is $3.0+9.0=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.B: Reverses the series voltage ratio, assigning 1.0 V to the single resistor.

perOption.C: The fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
perOption.D: The sixth order would also require $\sin\theta>1$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The total charge is $Q=It=(20\times10^{-3})(5.0)=0.10\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the magnitude of the electron charge gives $N=0.10/(1.6\times10^{-19})=6.3\times10^{17}$.

perOption.A: Gives the transferred charge in coulombs before dividing by the elementary charge.
perOption.B: Fails to convert the current-time product into an electron count using the elementary charge.
perOption.C: Correct. Divide the transferred charge by the charge magnitude per electron.
perOption.D: This many electrons would carry far more than the transferred $0.10\ \mathrm{C}$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The potential difference across $R$ is $IR$, so $IR=E-Ir$. The measurements give $3.0=E-1.0r$ and $4.8=E-0.4r$. Solving simultaneously gives $r=3.0\ \Omega$ and $E=6.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Predicts too small a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.
perOption.B: Correct. This resistance satisfies both readings with the same e.m.f.
perOption.C: Confuses the numerical value of the e.m.f. in volts with the internal resistance in ohms.
perOption.D: Predicts too large a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The right-hand network has equivalent capacitance $(1/C+1/C)^{-1}+C=1.5C$. It is in series with X, so it also carries $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and has voltage $V_{\mathrm{right}}=(6\ \mu\mathrm{C})/(1.5C)$. The lower branch has capacitance $C/2$, giving charge $(C/2)V_{\mathrm{right}}=2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. The two series capacitors in that branch carry equal charge, so Y stores $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Y carries the charge of the lower series branch.
perOption.B: Splits the charge equally between parallel branches with different capacitances.
perOption.C: Gives the charge on the single capacitor in the upper branch.
perOption.D: Treats Y as directly in series with X and ignores the upper branch.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The time constant is $\tau=RC=4700\times2200\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $E=\tfrac12 CV^2$, $E_0/E_t=(V_0/V_t)^2=8$ and $V_0/V_t=\sqrt{8}$. Substitution into $V_t=V_0e^{-t/\tau}$ gives $1/\sqrt{8}=e^{-t/\tau}$, so $t=10.8\ \mathrm{s}\approx11\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The voltage falls to $V_0/\sqrt{8}$.
perOption.B: At 16 s the energy has already fallen below one-eighth of its initial value.
perOption.C: Uses one-eighth as the voltage fraction, leaving one-sixty-fourth of the initial energy.
perOption.D: Treats the energy decrease as requiring three full $RC$ time constants.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The field pushes positive charges to the right and negative charges to the left. In B, the forces on each horizontal pair are equal, opposite and collinear. The net force is zero and the clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the centre balance.

perOption.A: The net rightward force on the top row and net leftward force on the bottom row produce moments in the same sense.
perOption.B: Correct. The resultant force and resultant moment are both zero.
perOption.C: The top and bottom charges experience unequal leftward forces, so their opposing moments do not cancel.
perOption.D: The rightward top forces and leftward bottom forces turn the square in the same sense.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The electric force must act upwards to balance the weight, so the upper plate is at lower potential. When $V$ is decreased, the particle falls towards the higher-potential lower plate. During that fall, the positive particle gains electric potential energy and loses gravitational potential energy.

perOption.A: During the fall, the positive particle moves towards higher electric potential.
perOption.B: Correct. During the fall, electric potential energy rises and gravitational potential energy falls.
perOption.C: During the rise, the positive particle moves towards lower electric potential.
perOption.D: After the voltage changes, the electric force and weight differ, so the energy changes need not have equal magnitudes.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The key compares positions during motion after the voltage adjustment. If the comparison includes the adjustment itself, the electric potential change depends on how the individual plate potentials are changed relative to a fixed reference.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The electron is negatively charged, so its electric force points along B. The magnetic force must point along D for the beam to remain undeflected. Fleming's left-hand rule, with conventional current opposite to the electron beam, gives magnetic field direction C.

perOption.A: This field reverses the magnetic force, making it reinforce the electric force.
perOption.B: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to B and could not oppose the electric force along B.
perOption.C: Correct. Field direction C produces a magnetic force along D.
perOption.D: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to D, although the required force is along D.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: By Lenz's law the coil end X becomes a north pole when north approaches and a south pole when south approaches, reversing the current and the needle deflection. At half the speed, the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller.

perOption.A: Accounts for the smaller deflection but misses the reversal caused by switching poles.
perOption.B: Correct. The needle moves less than 10 units to the right.
perOption.C: Misses both the current reversal and the decrease in magnitude.
perOption.D: Gets the reversal right but treats slower insertion as producing a larger current.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: Treat PQ as a straight conductor moving in the magnetic field. Fleming's right-hand rule gives conventional current from P to Q along the disc. The rotating disc acts as a source, so current flows internally from lower to higher potential and P is at lower potential than Q.

perOption.A: Correct. The disc drives current from P to Q with Q at higher potential.
perOption.B: Gets the polarity right but reverses the current inside the source.
perOption.C: Reverses both the induced current and the polarity.
perOption.D: Gets the current direction right but applies a resistor's potential drop to the source.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Over one period, $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4^2\times1+2^2\times2+0\times1)/4}=2.45\ \mathrm{A}$. The average power is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R=2.45^2\times11=66\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero mean current, although power depends on the mean squared current.
perOption.B: Uses the 2 A level alone and ignores the other parts of the waveform.
perOption.C: Correct. The period average of $I^2R$ is 66 W.
perOption.D: Counts the 4 A pulse but omits the power from the negative-current interval.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The de Broglie equation is $\lambda=h/p$. Therefore $\lambda p=h$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

perOption.A: Correct. The product is Planck's constant.
perOption.B: Makes wavelength directly proportional to momentum.
perOption.C: Substitutes kinetic energy for momentum, although the two are not proportional.
perOption.D: Makes wavelength increase with kinetic energy, although it decreases as momentum increases.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The graph of $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$ shows the position probability density. D has the narrowest peak, centred near $x=1.5$, and hence the smallest position uncertainty $\Delta x$. This gives the largest lower bound on $\Delta p$, which is the key's basis for choosing D.

perOption.A: The flat density spreads the particle across the region shown, giving weak localisation.
perOption.B: The probability is distributed across many peaks, giving a large position uncertainty.
perOption.C: The broad packet from about $x=0.0$ to $3.2$ gives a larger position uncertainty than D.
perOption.D: Correct. D is the most tightly localised in position.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key treats the uncertainty bound as an inverse equality. For standard deviations the bound is $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$. The graphs omit the wavefunction phase, so the densities alone cannot establish a ranking of momentum uncertainties. D is the intended answer.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Let R be the intermediate nucleus. Beta decay gives $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{P}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}+{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$, followed by gamma decay $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Q}+\gamma$. The neutron number in Q is $A-(Z+1)=A-Z-1$.

perOption.A: Correct. The neutron count drops by just one.
perOption.B: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and gamma emission leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.C: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and beta-minus decay converts one more into a proton.
perOption.D: Each beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so the count drops by two.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Let $C$ be the initial count rate due to the source alone. After two half-lives it has fallen by $3C/4$, so $3C/4=324-108$ and $C=288\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $324-288=36\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Quarters the later reading even though it includes a constant background contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The background contributes 36 counts per minute.
perOption.C: Halves the later reading even though the half-life applies only to the source contribution.
perOption.D: Gives the remaining source count rate after two half-lives.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: For $x=ab^2/c$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta x/x=\Delta a/a+2\Delta b/b+\Delta c/c$. In percentage terms, option A gives $(4+2(2)+4)\%=12\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $20\%$.
perOption.C: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $9\%$.
perOption.D: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $14\%$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The velocity of P relative to Q is $\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+(-\mathbf v_Q)$. Add the $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ westward vector to the tip of the $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ northward vector to obtain the steep northwest arrow.

perOption.A: Points southeast and understates the north–south component.
perOption.B: Points northwest but understates the northward component relative to the westward component.
perOption.C: Reverses the relative velocity and shows Q moving relative to P.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The complete sheet and the cut-out have centres $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M, respectively. Subtract the cut-out's first moment from the complete sheet's, giving $\rho tg[(4.0)(4.0)(2.0)-(1.0)(2.0)(3.0)]=26\rho tg$, using centimetres throughout. The remaining weight times its distance $y$ below M is $14\rho tg\,y$, so $y=26/14=1.857\ \mathrm{cm}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Shifts the centre too far upward for a cut-out of area $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shifts the centre toward the cut-out, as if the removed metal added weight.
perOption.D: Shifts the centre downward despite the removal of metal below the original centre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key labels the calculation as torques about M. The weights act along the vertical symmetry line through M, so the calculation uses first moments of weight with respect to depth below M.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The magnetic force $NBIL$ on the lowest side acts horizontally to the right. Balancing moments about the pivot gives $Mg(L/2)\sin 30^\circ=NBIL(L\cos 30^\circ)$. Substituting $0.30(0.025)\sin 30^\circ=100B(0.40)(0.050)(0.050)\cos 30^\circ$ gives $B=0.043\ \mathrm T$.

perOption.A: Omits the $\cos 30^\circ$ factor from the magnetic force's moment arm.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor from the weight's moment arm.
perOption.D: Uses the full side length in the weight's moment arm.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: By $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, the constant positive force produces constant acceleration, so velocity increases along a straight line. When the net force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity–time graph is horizontal.

perOption.A: Copies the force pulse and shows instantaneous changes in velocity.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows deceleration after the force has dropped to zero.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration during a constant force.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The cart has a forward tension $T$ and a backward resistive force of $40\ \mathrm N$. Newton's second law gives $T-40=600(0.15)$, so $T=130\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: A tension of $65\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $25\ \mathrm N$ to accelerate the cart.
perOption.B: A tension of $100\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $60\ \mathrm N$ of net force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A tension of $195\ \mathrm N$ gives $155\ \mathrm N$ of net force, exceeding the required $90\ \mathrm N$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The useful output power is $Fv=1600(11)=17\,600\ \mathrm W$, all of which goes into overcoming resistance at constant speed on level ground. The fuel supplies $1.8\times10^6/60=30\,000\ \mathrm W$. The efficiency is $(17\,600/30\,000)\times100\%\approx59\%$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the ratio of the $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful power to the $30.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ fuel input.
perOption.B: At the stated fuel input, this percentage accounts for only about $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ of useful power.
perOption.C: This percentage treats the roughly $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful output as only a little over a third of the $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ input.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The total energy is the initial kinetic energy $E=\tfrac12mu^2$. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, but the constant horizontal velocity is $u\cos60^\circ=u/2$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m(u/2)^2=E/4$. By energy conservation, the gravitational potential energy there is $3E/4$, so the two curves cross.

perOption.A: Shows zero kinetic energy at the top, as for a vertical launch.
perOption.B: Shows equal energies at the top, as for a $45^\circ$ launch.
perOption.C: Keeps kinetic energy above half the total, as for a launch below $45^\circ$.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Take right as positive and let $V$ be P's final velocity. In an elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, so $v-0=0.4v-V$. Thus $V=-0.6v$ and P's speed is $0.6v$.

perOption.A: Stopping P would leave a separation speed of only $0.4v$.
perOption.B: Even if P rebounds at $0.4v$, the separation speed would be only $0.8v$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: If P rebounded at $v$, the separation speed would be $1.4v$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The centripetal acceleration is $a=r\omega^2=r(2\pi/T)^2$. With $r=7.70\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m$ and $T=2.36\ \mathrm s$, this gives $a=0.546\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the acceleration by using too small a value for the squared angular speed.
perOption.B: The value is $r\omega$, which is the tangential speed in metres per second.
perOption.C: Underestimates the acceleration given by multiplying the radius by the squared angular speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The gravitational field is perpendicular to the equipotential through X, leaving A and C as candidates. Since $g=-\mathrm d\phi/\mathrm dx$ along the normal, the field points toward decreasing potential, from $-300$ toward $-400\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.
perOption.C: Points toward increasing gravitational potential.
perOption.D: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: The potential is $-GM/r$, so doubling P's distance halves the potential magnitude to $\phi/2$. The inverse-distance curve is steeper nearer the mass, so moving P and Q outward by the same distance reduces the potential magnitude at P by more than at Q. The magnitude of the potential difference therefore decreases.

perOption.A: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much for a doubling of distance.
perOption.B: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much and assumes P and Q change by equal amounts.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes equal outward shifts cause equal potential changes.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: At $t=0$, acceleration is zero, so the particle is at equilibrium and its kinetic energy is maximum. Acceleration is zero three times from $t=0$ to $2\ \mathrm s$ inclusive, so the kinetic energy has three maxima in that interval.

perOption.A: Misses the kinetic-energy peak at the middle equilibrium crossing.
perOption.B: Shows zero kinetic energy at the initial and final equilibrium crossings.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts kinetic-energy minima at the equilibrium crossings.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The pulse takes $0.25/0.50=0.5\ \mathrm s$ to travel $0.25\ \mathrm m$. Its leading edge reaches O at $1.0\ \mathrm s$, where the fixed end reflects and inverts the pulse. By $1.5\ \mathrm s$ that edge has travelled $0.75\ \mathrm m$ and reached P on its return. As the reflected pulse passes P between $1.5$ and $2.0\ \mathrm s$, P moves first through a larger upward displacement and then a smaller downward one.

perOption.A: Shows the smaller upward displacement first, reversing the order of the reflected lobes.
perOption.B: Shows the incoming pulse's displacement sequence, missing the inversion at the fixed end.
perOption.C: Inverts the lobes but puts the trailing lobe first.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: At distance $r$ from the source, the intensity is $I=P_s/(4\pi r^2)$. The surface receives $P=IA$, so for fixed area $P\propto P_s/r^2$. Doubling both $P_s$ and $r$ gives $P_R/P_S=2/2^2=1/2$, so $P_R=0.70\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square decrease but misses the doubling of source power.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-distance law, making the two doublings cancel.
perOption.D: Doubles the received power without accounting for the greater distance.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The third-order maxima are symmetric, so each is at $\theta=60^\circ/2=30^\circ$ to the central direction. With line density $N=1/d$, the grating equation $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $N=\sin30^\circ/(3\times500\times10^{-9})=3.33\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. This is $333$ lines per millimetre.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses an incorrect sine factor for the $30^\circ$ diffraction angle.
perOption.C: Drops the factor $\sin30^\circ=0.5$ from the line-density calculation.
perOption.D: Reports the line count per metre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Using Rayleigh's criterion in the form $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, take $b=2.4\ \mathrm m$ and a typical visible wavelength $\lambda=500\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm m$. The stars are just resolved, so their separation is $\theta_{\min}\approx(500\times10^{-9})/2.4\approx2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the diffraction limit by more than an order of magnitude.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 50.
perOption.D: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 100.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The key uses the order-of-magnitude form of Rayleigh's criterion. Including the circular-aperture factor of 1.22 still gives B.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Internal energy is a state property, so its change depends only on states A and B. Along A–C–B, the first law gives $\Delta U=Q+W_{\mathrm{on}}=16-6=10\ \mathrm J$. Along A–D–B, $10=Q-2$, so $Q=+12\ \mathrm J$ and heat enters the gas.

perOption.A: Reverses the sign of the internal energy change and treats work done by the gas as work done on it.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes that heat transfer is the same along both paths.
perOption.D: Adds the $4\ \mathrm J$ difference in work to the original heat input even though the gas does less work.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water. With equilibrium temperature $\theta$, density $\rho$ and specific heat capacity $c$, this gives $120\rho c(60-\theta)=30\rho c(\theta-20)$. Cancelling the common factors gives $4(60-\theta)=\theta-20$, so $5\theta=260$ and $\theta=52^\circ\mathrm C$.

perOption.A: Weights the mixture too heavily toward the cold water despite the hot water having four times its mass.
perOption.B: Reverses the hot and cold mass weights, giving the cold water four times the influence.
perOption.C: Underweights the hot water, which has four times the mass of the cold water.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The field from $+2q$ is $E_{2q}=2q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.30)^2]=24\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ to the right. The field from $-q$ is also to the right and has magnitude $q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.60)^2]=E_{2q}/8=3\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. Adding the two gives $27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the fields and treats the charge magnitudes as equal.
perOption.B: Subtracts the field of the negative charge even though both fields point right.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the charges as equal in magnitude, doubling the negative charge's contribution.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For each wire, $I=enAv=en(\pi d^2/4)v$. The wires are in series, so $I_X=I_Y$ and $n_Xd_X^2v_X=n_Yd_Y^2v_Y$. Hence $v_Y=(n_X/n_Y)(d_X/d_Y)^2v_X=2(1/2)^2(0.52)=0.26\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the diameter ratio directly as the area ratio.
perOption.C: Accounts for the density ratio alone and ignores the different areas.
perOption.D: Inverts the area ratio and omits the density ratio.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The voltmeter reads highest when the fixed resistor has the smallest potential difference. By the potential-divider principle, this happens when the combined resistance of the thermistor and LDR is greatest. Low temperature increases the NTC thermistor’s resistance, and low brightness increases the LDR’s resistance.

perOption.A: High temperature and high brightness both lower the measured pair’s resistance.
perOption.B: High temperature lowers the NTC thermistor’s resistance.
perOption.C: High brightness lowers the LDR’s resistance.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The worked solution swaps the temperature and brightness dependencies and incorrectly says the LDR resistance should be low. The explanation corrects those slips using the same potential-divider method.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The two parallel $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors give $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. This combination is in series with the other two $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors, so $C_{\mathrm{eq}}=(1/4+1/4+1/4)^{-1}\ \mu\mathrm{F}=1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. The battery circulates $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=(1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F})(12\ \mathrm{V})=16\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Counts only the two standalone $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors in series.
perOption.C: Assumes an equivalent capacitance of $3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, which the parallel-then-series reduction does not give.
perOption.D: Implies an equivalent capacitance of about $9.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, even though the series combination must be below $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The instantaneous power is $P=I_0^2R\sin^2(\omega t)$, so the graph has smooth minima at zero. The mean power is $\langle P\rangle=I^2R$. The peak is twice the mean, giving $P_0=2I^2R=2I^2(2)=4I^2$.

perOption.A: The sharp minima resemble a rectified sine rather than a squared sine.
perOption.B: The curve has the right shape but peaks at $\sqrt{2}I^2$ instead of $4I^2$.
perOption.C: Uses the mean power as the peak.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: In B, the magnetic force on the upward-moving electron points left, and the electric force points out of the page. Both forces are transverse to the path and point in perpendicular directions, so they cannot cancel. The resulting transverse force deflects the electron from the straight path.

perOption.A: The magnetic field is parallel to the velocity, so only the electric force acts, accelerating the electron along the path.
perOption.B: Correct. The transverse forces cannot cancel.
perOption.C: The key treats C as possible by balancing lateral forces, but the upward electric force changes the speed and breaks that balance.
perOption.D: The electric force into the page can balance the magnetic force out of the page.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.issues: Both B and C are impossible for the full path in uniform fields. In C, the upward electric force changes the electron’s speed, so the speed-dependent rightward magnetic force can balance the constant leftward electric component only instantaneously. B is a valid choice, but the question has no unique correct letter.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The flux cut is $\Delta\Phi=BA=BL(vt)$. In $30\ \mathrm{s}$, the rod sweeps out $A=0.24(0.50\times30)=3.6\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The flux cut is therefore $0.15\times3.6=0.54\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Gives the flux cut in one second.
perOption.B: Gives the flux cut in two seconds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a full minute instead of half a minute.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Intensity equals the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time multiplied by the energy per photon. The beams have the same frequency, so their photons carry the same energy. The more intense beam therefore has more photons crossing unit area each second.

perOption.A: Equal frequencies give equal photon energies.
perOption.B: All photons travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
perOption.C: Amplitude describes the electric and magnetic field oscillations in the wave picture.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The slit confines the electron in the transverse $y$ direction, so $\Delta y$ is defined at the slit. The electrons spread in $y$ as they pass through, giving a transverse momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$. The uncertainty principle pairs position and momentum along the same axis.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Places both uncertainties at the screen, although the slit sets the position uncertainty used here.
perOption.C: Pairs a transverse position uncertainty with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.
perOption.D: Uses the screen for the position uncertainty and pairs it with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: In $\beta^-$ decay, a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. The proton number rises from $94$ to $95$, and the neutron number falls from $145$ to $144$. This is one square right and one square down from X, at B.

From the diagram, the wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next (or one rarefaction to the next): $\lambda = 16\ \mathrm{m}$.

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{16}{16} = 1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The second-order lines are $56°$ apart, so each is at $\theta = 28°$: $d\sin 28° = 2\lambda \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°}$.

From $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and $\sin\theta \le 1$: $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°} = 4.26$, so $n_{\max} = 4$.

Number of diffraction lines $= (4 \times 2) + 1 = 9$

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Distance $r = 20 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$. By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \lambda/D$, so the minimum separation is $s = r\theta = r\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$.

Violet (400 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(400 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 2.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Red (700 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(700 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 4.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

perOption.B: Correct. $s = r\lambda/D \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for visible light.

perOption.D: Far too large. It does not follow from $s = r\lambda/D$ with visible wavelengths.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac{1}{2}M\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so

$\dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}M_P c_P^2}{\tfrac{1}{2}M_Q c_Q^2} = \dfrac{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_P}{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_Q}$

$\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q} = \dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} \times \dfrac{c_Q^2}{c_P^2} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

perOption.B: Correct. $M \propto T/c^2$.
perOption.C: Forgets to square the r.m.s. speed ratio.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
By the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q + W$, where $W$ is the work done on the gas.

Heat supplied to the gas: $Q = \Delta U - W$

So the heat transferred from the gas to the surroundings is $W - \Delta U$.

perOption.A: Adds $\Delta U$ to $W$, as if the rise in internal energy also leaves the gas as heat.
perOption.B: Correct. Heat lost $= -Q = W - \Delta U$.
perOption.C: This is the heat supplied to the gas, $Q = \Delta U - W$, not the heat it loses.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^3 \Rightarrow V \propto d^3$, so $V_f = \left(\dfrac{2d}{d}\right)^3 V = 8V$.

$\Delta V = 8V - V = 7V$

$W = p\Delta V = 7pV$

perOption.B: Uses a factor of 4, the change in surface area, instead of in volume.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Let $r$ be the side of one grid square. The 32.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $r$ from Q:

$E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} = 32.0$

S is $3r$ from Q: $E_S = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (3r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{9}(32.0) = 3.6\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

Check: the 16.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $\sqrt{2}r$ away, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}E = 16.0\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

R is $\sqrt{(2r)^2 + r^2} = \sqrt{5}r$ away: $E_R = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(\sqrt{5}r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{5}E = 6.4\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

perOption.D: Uses $E \propto 1/r$ or miscounts the distances, rather than $E \propto 1/r^2$ with the correct geometry.

Outside the sphere, the potential decreases inversely with the distance $x$ from the centre: $V \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$.
