perOption.C: The expansion area exceeds the compression area, so the net work done on the gas is negative.
perOption.D: Internal energy depends on the state, and the gas returns to its initial state.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: By the first law, $\Delta U=\frac32nR\Delta T=Q+W_{\mathrm{on}}$. In the first case $\frac32nR\Delta T_1=1000-500=500\ \mathrm J$, and in the second $\frac32nR\Delta T_2=2000-500=1500\ \mathrm J$. Hence $\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2=500/1500=0.33$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the work in the first case but adds it in the second, giving $500/2500$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Takes the ratio of the heat inputs alone and omits the work.
perOption.D: Adds the work done by the gas to the heat input, giving $1500/2500$.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: From $pV=nRT$, the fixed cylinder volume and limiting pressure give $n_1RT_1=n_2RT_2$. With molar mass $M_{\mathrm r}$, this is $\frac{m_1}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_1=\frac{m_2}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_2$. Thus $m_2=\frac{273.15+10}{273.15+30}(15)=14.0\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Uses inverse proportionality with temperatures in degrees Celsius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes the mass directly proportional to absolute temperature.
perOption.D: Makes the mass directly proportional to the Celsius temperature.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: At distance $d$, $V=Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0d)$ and $E=Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0d^2)$. Replacing $d$ by $d/4$ gives $V_{\mathrm{new}}=Q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(d/4)]=4V$. The field becomes $E_{\mathrm{new}}=Q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(d/4)^2]=16E$.

perOption.A: Uses 8 as the field multiplier instead of squaring the distance factor of 4.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overstates the potential multiplier and understates the inverse-square increase in field strength.
perOption.D: Applies a factor of 8 to the potential even though it scales inversely with distance.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The electric field is the negative potential gradient, $E=-\mathrm dV/\mathrm dx$. The potential gradient is negative throughout, so the field is positive. Near the middle the slope has its smallest magnitude and remains nonzero, so the field has a positive minimum.

perOption.A: Confuses the zero of potential with a zero of its gradient.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong field sign and gives zero at a point where the slope remains nonzero.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the potential gradient itself, giving a negative field.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key's phrase “minimum gradient” refers to the smallest gradient magnitude. The graphs also show finite endpoint values, whereas ideal point-charge potential and field diverge at the charge positions. C matches the intended trend between the charges.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The electrons and positive mercury ions move in opposite directions, so their conventional currents add. In one minute the effective charge transferred is $Q=(1.5\times10^{15}+4.4\times10^{15})(1.6\times10^{-19})=9.44\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm C$. Thus $I=Q/t=(9.44\times10^{-4})/60=1.57\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm A\approx16\ \mu\mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the charge-carrier counts even though both streams contribute current in the same direction.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Subtracts the two charge contributions and treats the one-minute charge as a per-second flow.
perOption.D: Treats the total charge crossing in one minute as if it crossed in one second.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For cell voltage $V$, the series capacitance is $C/3$, so $Q_1=CV/3$. The parallel capacitance is $3C$, so $Q_2=3CV$. Hence $Q_1/Q_2=(CV/3)/(3CV)=1/9$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Accounts for the factor of three in only one of the two combinations.
perOption.C: Uses a single factor of three in the reverse direction.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio of series charge to parallel charge.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Power is $P=V^2/R$, so for identical resistors $P\propto V^2$. Q and R are in parallel and S carries twice either branch current, giving $V_S:V_R:V_Q=2:1:1$. Squaring gives a power ratio of $4:1:1$, so R dissipates $\frac16(12)=2\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Allocates power in proportion to voltage, giving R one part out of four.
perOption.C: Divides the total power equally among all three resistors based on their equal resistances.
perOption.D: Assigns to R the four-sixths power share that belongs to S.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
$V_T$ measures the fixed resistor’s voltage, so a high reading means a low voltage across the thermistor. This requires a low thermistor resistance, which occurs at high temperature.

$V_L$ measures the LDR’s voltage, so a high reading requires a high LDR resistance, which occurs at low light level.

perOption.A: Low temperature raises the thermistor resistance and lowers $V_T$.
perOption.B: Low temperature lowers $V_T$, and bright light lowers $V_L$.
perOption.C: Correct. Both readings are high.
perOption.D: Bright light lowers the LDR resistance and hence $V_L$.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The electron moves right, so the equivalent conventional current points left. With the field out of the paper, Fleming’s left-hand rule gives an upward force at entry. The force stays perpendicular to the motion, producing an upward-curving circular path.

perOption.A: Curves downward as a positive charge would.
perOption.B: Shows a straight deflection even though the magnetic force continuously changes the direction of motion.
perOption.C: Assumes zero force even though the electron moves perpendicular to the field.
perOption.D: Correct. The electron initially curves upward.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: Take moments about the knife edge. At equilibrium the moment of the weight balances that of the magnetic force, so $(mg)q=(BIL)p$. Rearranging gives $B=\frac{mgq}{ILp}$.

perOption.A: Uses the whole side length $p+q$ as the length of wire in the field.
perOption.B: Uses the full side length $p+q$ and substitutes mass for weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight and magnetic force produce equal opposing moments.
perOption.D: Omits $g$ when converting the hanging mass to weight.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: For the rotating disc, the centre-to-rim e.m.f. is $E=BAf=B\pi r^2 f$. Q and S are both at radius $r/2$, where the enclosed area is one quarter of the disc area, so each centre-to-point e.m.f. has magnitude $E/4$. Along Q to O to S, the two radial e.m.f.s have opposite signs and cancel.

perOption.A: Correct. Q and S are at the same potential.
perOption.B: Gives the e.m.f. between O and either midpoint.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes along QOS even though the contributions have opposite signs.
perOption.D: Uses the centre-to-rim e.m.f. for two points at the same radius.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.issues: The question prints ‘placed is’ for ‘placed in’. The key’s opposite-polarity wording applies to traversing Q→O and O→S. Both points have the same polarity relative to O.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: For the ideal transformer, $\frac{N_p}{N_s}=\frac{V_p}{V_s}=\frac{I_s}{I_p}=\frac{120}{4.0}=30$. Hence $N_p=30(240)=7200$ turns. The output voltage is $V_s=450/30=15\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the current ratio for both the turns and the voltage.
perOption.B: Gets the voltage right but inverts the turns ratio.
perOption.C: Gets the turns right but multiplies $V_p$ by 30.
perOption.D: Correct. The primary has 7200 turns and the output is 15 V.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: Both particles start from rest and gain kinetic energy $K=|q||\Delta V|$. The charge magnitudes and the magnitudes of the potential differences are equal, giving equal kinetic energies. Combining $\lambda=h/p$ with $p^2/(2m)=K$ gives $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2m|q||\Delta V|}$. The heavier proton therefore has the shorter wavelength.

perOption.A: Assigns the electron more energy and reverses the wavelength comparison.
perOption.B: Assigns the proton more energy even though both particles gain equal energy.
perOption.C: Reverses the momentum comparison at fixed kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The lighter electron has the longer wavelength.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key describes the charges as the same. Their magnitudes are equal and their signs are opposite.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: From 0 to 50 s the measured count rate falls by $72-40=32\ \mathrm{Bq}$. Only the source contribution decays, so the drop halves in each successive half-life. From 50 to 100 s it falls by $16\ \mathrm{Bq}$ to $24\ \mathrm{Bq}$, then from 100 to 150 s by $8\ \mathrm{Bq}$ to $16\ \mathrm{Bq}$.

perOption.A: Gives the source contribution at 150 s and omits the background.
perOption.B: Correct. The measured rate is 16 Bq.
perOption.C: Stops at the count rate for 100 s.
perOption.D: Uses the first 50 s drop as the final count rate.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The paper labels measured count rate in Bq, and the key calls it activity. Detector count rate is conventionally stated in counts per unit time.

tmjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Along the chain, each alpha decay reduces the mass number by 4 and the proton number by 2, and each beta-minus decay increases the proton number by 1. The final nuclide shown is lead-212 with proton number 82, giving $212-82=130$ neutrons.

perOption.A: Correct. Lead-212 has 130 neutrons.
perOption.B: Gives the neutron number before the last two alpha decays.
perOption.C: Gives the lead mass number instead of its neutron number.
perOption.D: Gives the mass number of the radon intermediate.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Equate the base units in $E=Q^n/(2k)$. This gives $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}=(\mathrm{A^n\,s^n})/(\mathrm{A^2\,s^4\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-2}})$. The ampere exponent on the right is $n-2$, so $n=2$.

perOption.A: Leaves an ampere exponent of $-4$.
perOption.B: Leaves an ampere exponent of $-3$.
perOption.C: Leaves an ampere exponent of $-1$.
perOption.D: Correct. Squaring the charge cancels the ampere units.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Y is height: it starts above zero with zero slope, and the magnitude of its slope increases to the constant terminal speed. Z is speed: it starts at zero and levels off at terminal speed. X is the resultant force: it starts at the weight because drag is initially zero, then falls to zero as drag rises to equal the weight.

perOption.A: Assigns Y to speed even though it starts above zero, and Z to force even though it starts at zero.
perOption.B: Uses X for height even though it starts with a steep slope, and Y for force even though it fails to fall to zero as Z levels off.
perOption.C: Uses Z for height even though it starts at zero, and Y for speed even though it starts above zero.
perOption.D: Correct. Height, speed and resultant force correspond to Y, Z and X respectively.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: A person feels weightless in free fall when gravity alone acts on them. While the athlete clears the bar, gravity is the only appreciable force.

perOption.A: Correct. The athlete is in free fall.
perOption.B: The water exerts an upward buoyant force.
perOption.C: The parachute harness exerts an upward force on the parachutist.
perOption.D: The seat exerts an upward normal force on the pilot.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: If you push an object and static friction balances your push, the object stays still. With zero displacement, the work done against friction and the energy dissipated are both zero.

perOption.A: Work done against friction depends on the path taken.
perOption.B: A falling object can hit the ground before reaching terminal speed.
perOption.C: Friction between our feet and the ground allows us to move forward.
perOption.D: Correct. Static friction can act while the object stays still.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Work is the component of the pulling force along the sled’s motion multiplied by the distance moved. Thus $W=(20.0\cos 30^\circ)(40)\approx692.8\ \mathrm{J}$, which rounds to $690\ \mathrm{J}$ at the precision of the options.

perOption.A: Uses the vertical component $20.0sin30^circ$ for horizontal motion.
perOption.B: Uses an effective horizontal force of about $12.3 mathrm{N}$, below the actual $20.0cos30^circ$.
perOption.C: Correct. Only the horizontal force component does work on the sled.
perOption.D: Uses the full $20.0 mathrm{N}$ without projecting it along the displacement.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The key prints 692 J for an intermediate result of 692.82… J. The listed answer of 690 J is correct.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The spring length increases from $7.5$ to $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ while the force increases from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm{N}$. The work is the trapezoidal area between the line and the length axis over that interval. This gives $W=\tfrac12(3.0+6.0)(10.0-7.5)\times10^{-2}=0.11\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct. The trapezoid uses the initial and final forces over the extra extension.
perOption.B: Uses the final force of 6.0 N throughout the extra extension.
perOption.C: Takes the area against the force axis using the mean length and the change in force.
perOption.D: Takes the entire trapezoid against the force axis from 0 to 6.0 N.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: When the string just slackens, its tension is zero, so the inward component of the weight provides the centripetal force. Thus $mg\cos\theta=mv_B^2/r$, giving $\theta=\cos^{-1}[2.2^2/(1.5\times9.81)]=71^\circ$.

perOption.A: Places the string almost vertical, where the radial component of weight would be too large.
perOption.B: Uses the angle complementary to the one measured from the vertical.
perOption.C: Correct. The radial component of weight alone supplies the centripetal force.
perOption.D: Places the string too close to horizontal, giving too small a radial component of weight.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: For a circular orbit of radius $d$, gravity provides the centripetal force, so $GMm/d^2=mv^2/d$. This gives $v=\sqrt{GM/d}$ and $K=\tfrac12mv^2=GMm/(2d)$. Q is slower because its orbit is larger, but doubling both the satellite mass and the orbital radius leaves $K$ equal to $GMm/(2r)$ for each satellite.

perOption.A: Reverses the radius dependence of orbital speed.
perOption.B: Overlooks the dependence of orbital speed on radius.
perOption.C: Counts Q’s greater mass without accounting for its lower speed.
perOption.D: Correct. Both satellites have the same mass-to-orbital-radius ratio.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: The displacement curve starts at its positive maximum, so velocity follows a negative sine curve and acceleration follows a negative cosine curve. At C the velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive, so the body is travelling and accelerating in opposite directions.

perOption.A: Velocity and acceleration are both negative.
perOption.B: Acceleration is zero as the body passes through equilibrium.
perOption.C: Correct. The velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive.
perOption.D: Velocity is zero at the turning point.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: From the graph, $U=1.0\ \mathrm{J}$ at $x=0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. Using the SHM energy relation and $\omega=2\pi/T$ gives $1.0=\tfrac12(4.0)(2\pi/T)^2(0.2)^2$. Solving gives $T=1.78\ \mathrm{s}$, or $1.8\ \mathrm{s}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Gives a period that predicts a potential energy far above 1.0 J at the marked displacement.
perOption.B: Halves the calculated full period.
perOption.C: Correct. The energy–position pair gives a period of about 1.8 s.
perOption.D: Is consistent with omitting the factor of one half in the energy formula.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.issues: The key uses total-energy notation with amplitude. The graph supplies a potential-energy value at a displacement, which gives the same calculation directly.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/20\ \mathrm{s}=50\ \mathrm{ms}$. The wavelength spans eight divisions, and the right-moving zero crossing immediately to the left of Q is one division away. This is a phase difference of $\Delta\phi=2\pi/8=\pi/4$, so $\Delta t=(\Delta\phi/2\pi)T=6.25\ \mathrm{ms}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The first zero crossing reaches Q in one eighth of a period.
perOption.B: Uses the zero crossing three divisions to the right of Q, which moves away.
perOption.C: Uses the second zero crossing to arrive, five divisions to the left of Q.
perOption.D: Uses seven eighths of a period for a shift of only one division.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.issues: The key calls the upstream zero crossing P, but the diagram labels only Q.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: By Malus’ law the detected intensity is $I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $I_0$ is the reading for parallel axes. A 36% reduction leaves $0.64I_0$, so $\cos^2\theta=0.64$. This gives $\theta=36.9^\circ$, or about $37^\circ$.

perOption.A: Transmits about 85% of the original reading, a drop of only about 15%.
perOption.B: Correct. About 64% of the original reading remains.
perOption.C: Transmits about 41% of the original reading, a drop of about 59%.
perOption.D: Treats the 36% lost as the fraction transmitted.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
Use $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ with $n=1$ and $d=1/(4.0\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. The blue end at $420\ \mathrm{nm}$ is at $9.67^\circ$ and the red end at $680\ \mathrm{nm}$ is at $15.8^\circ$.

Their separation is $15.8^\circ-9.67^\circ=6.13^\circ$, or $6.1^\circ$ to the precision of the options.

perOption.A: Correct. It is the difference between the two first-order angles.
perOption.B: Uses only the angle of the blue ray from the normal.
perOption.C: Uses only the angle of the red ray from the normal.
perOption.D: Adds the angles as if the rays were on opposite sides of the normal.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The first minimum satisfies $b\sin\theta=\lambda$, so $\theta\approx\lambda/b$ for small angles. At screen distance $D$, the central maximum has width $x\approx 2D\theta\approx 2D\lambda/b$. Bringing the screen closer decreases $D$ and therefore decreases $x$, so A is the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: Correct. Bringing the screen closer decreases $x$.
perOption.B: This statement is true because a wider slit lets more light through.
perOption.C: This statement is true because increasing $b$ reduces $x$.
perOption.D: This statement is true because increasing $\lambda$ increases $x$.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The key’s comment for option D says that increasing wavelength decreases the width. Its equation shows that the width increases.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Melting requires $Q_1=mL_f$ and vaporization requires $Q_2=mL_v$. At constant heating power $P$, the energies supplied during the plateaus are $Pt_1$ and $Pt_2$. Thus $L_v/L_f=Q_2/Q_1=Pt_2/(Pt_1)=(25-11)/(6-2)=3.5$.

perOption.A: Assumes the two plateaus last equally long.
perOption.B: Divides the plateau temperatures, 300 K and about 125 K, instead of their durations.
perOption.C: Correct. The plateaus last 14 min and 4 min.
perOption.D: Uses the full 20 min from 6 min to 26 min and includes intervals where temperature rises.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, and the ideal-gas law gives $PV=NkT$. Combining them gives $c_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3PV/(Nm)}$, so for a fixed amount of gas $c_{\mathrm{rms}}\propto\sqrt{PV}$. Therefore $u'/u=\sqrt{(2P)(2V)/(PV)}=2$, giving $u'=2u$.

perOption.A: Treats $PV$ as unchanged when both factors double.
perOption.B: Accounts for doubling only one of pressure and volume.
perOption.C: Correct. The pressure–volume product quadruples.
perOption.D: Scales the r.m.s. speed directly with $PV$.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.issues: The solution assumes a fixed amount of gas, which the question leaves implicit.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, the internal energy remains constant, so $\Delta U=0$. Expansion gives $\Delta V>0$, so the work done on the gas is negative, as indicated by $W=-p\Delta V$. The first law $\Delta U=Q+W$ then gives $Q=-W>0$.

perOption.A: Correct. Heat supplied balances the work done by the gas.
perOption.B: Assigns positive internal-energy change and positive work on the gas to an isothermal expansion.
perOption.C: Reverses the signs of the work done on the gas and the heat supplied.
perOption.D: Assigns a decrease in internal energy to a gas whose temperature stays constant.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The final line of the key says W must be positive. It should say Q must be positive, consistent with option A.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The field along the displacement is $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x$. Between $3.0$ and $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$, the area under the graph is $\tfrac12(7.8+5.2)(5.0-3.0)=13\ \mathrm{V}$. The field points in the direction of increasing $x$, so the potential decreases and $\Delta V=-13\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The potential change is the negative of the trapezium area.
perOption.B: Uses the slope of the field graph as the potential change.
perOption.C: Uses the magnitude of the slope instead of the negative area.
perOption.D: Uses the area with the wrong sign.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The key treats E as the signed field component along x. If the plotted field strength meant only its magnitude, the direction and sign of the potential change would be unspecified.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The potential at X is the sum of the contributions from $+Q$ at $3d$ and $-2Q$ at $d$, so $V_X=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(3d)}+\frac{-2Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}=-\frac{5Q}{12\pi\varepsilon_0d}$. Multiplying by the charge placed at X gives $U=(3Q)V_X=-\frac{5Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$.

perOption.A: Uses the magnitude of the energy and loses the negative sign.
perOption.B: Correct. The negative source charge dominates the potential at X.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-square dependence for potential energy.
perOption.D: Uses an inverse-square dependence and gives a positive energy.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: Use $I=nAve$, where $n=N/(AL)$ for a wire with $N$ free electrons and length $L$. Substituting gives $I=Nve/L$. Hence $N=IL/(ve)=(12)(0.35)/[(5.0\times10^{-4})(1.6\times10^{-19})]=5.25\times10^{22}$, or $5.3\times10^{22}$.

perOption.A: Severely undercounts the electrons by retaining an area factor even though the area cancels.
perOption.B: Correct. The wire contains about $5.3\times10^{22}$ free electrons.
perOption.C: Omits the $0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ length factor, giving the number per metre.
perOption.D: Overcounts the electrons by using inconsistent factors for the wire dimensions where the area should cancel.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The voltmeter measures the voltage across the fixed resistor, so an increased reading means a larger current by $V_R=IR$. For the cell, $V_{\mathrm{terminal}}=\mathcal E-Ir$. The emf and internal resistance are fixed, so the larger current increases the internal voltage drop and decreases the terminal potential difference.

perOption.A: The charge per unit time is the current, which increases.
perOption.B: The energy transferred per unit charge is the voltage across the fixed resistor, which increases.
perOption.C: The LDR resistance falls as current increases, so incident light intensity must increase.
perOption.D: Correct. A larger current increases the internal voltage drop.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The magnetic force contributes a moment $BIL(0.240)$ and the hanging mass contributes an opposing moment $mg(0.320)$. By the principle of moments, these are equal. Therefore $B=\frac{(0.0150)(9.81)(0.320)}{(1.50)(0.180)(0.240)}=0.727\ \mathrm{T}$, or $0.73\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the magnetic moment required to balance the hanging mass.
perOption.B: Uses a magnetic moment too small to balance the mass at its $0.32\ \mathrm{m}$ lever arm.
perOption.C: Correct. The opposing moments balance at this flux density.
perOption.D: Overestimates the required magnetic force by assigning too large a moment to the hanging mass.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The magnetic force has magnitude $F=BIL\sin\theta$. The currents along AB and CD are parallel or antiparallel to the field, so the force on each is zero. BC and DA are perpendicular to the field and carry opposite currents, so their magnetic forces point in opposite directions.

perOption.A: Correct. The field is aligned with AB and CD.
perOption.B: BC and DA are perpendicular to the field, so both experience a force.
perOption.C: Opposite current directions give opposite force directions in the same field.
perOption.D: AB and CD experience zero force, while BC and DA experience nonzero forces.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Square the voltage graph to get $9.00\ \mathrm{V^2}$ for $1.00\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $4.00\ \mathrm{V^2}$ for $2.00\ \mathrm{ms}$ in each period. The mean square is $[9.00+2(4.00)]/3=5.6667\ \mathrm{V^2}$. Taking the square root gives an r.m.s. voltage of $2.38\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Applies the sinusoidal peak-to-r.m.s. factor to a rectangular waveform.
perOption.B: Correct. The squared voltage levels are weighted by their durations.
perOption.C: Averages the two voltage magnitudes directly and gives them equal weight.
perOption.D: Gives the two squared voltage levels equal weight even though their durations differ.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The motional emf is $\mathcal E=B_vlv=(5.0\times10^{-5})(17.0)(30)=0.0255\ \mathrm{V}$, which rounds to $26\ \mathrm{mV}$. For the polarity, the key uses Lenz’s law and Fleming’s left-hand rule to select the right-to-left direction for conventional current in the wing. The left wing is therefore at higher potential.

perOption.A: Misses the emf generated as the wing cuts the downward magnetic field.
perOption.B: Identifies the higher-potential wing but underestimates the emf from the given wingspan and speed.
perOption.C: Gets the emf magnitude but reverses its polarity.
perOption.D: Correct. The left wing is at higher potential.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.issues: The key’s intermediate 0.025 V is truncated from 0.0255 V. Its 26 mV result is correct. The current direction in the key refers to the induced emf polarity, since no closed circuit is specified.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: By Faraday’s law, $\mathcal E=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(NBA\cos\omega t)=\omega NBA\sin\omega t$. The maximum is therefore $(2\pi f)NBA$. Using $f=1800/60\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $A=\pi(1.0\times10^{-2})^2/4\ \mathrm{m^2}$ gives $\mathcal E_{\max}=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.
perOption.B: Uses $f$ in place of $\omega=2\pi f$.
perOption.C: Correct. The peak emf is $\omega NBA$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Squaring the magnitude of the wavefunction gives the probability density, $|\psi|^2$. The wavefunction has its largest magnitude at Q and S, so the probability density is highest at both positions.

perOption.A: Counts the positive peak but misses the equally large magnitude at the negative trough.
perOption.B: Correct. The squared magnitude is maximal at Q and S.
perOption.C: Includes P and R, where the wavefunction is zero.
perOption.D: Selects the nodes, where the probability density is zero.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The question’s probability at a position refers to probability density, as the key explains.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: From $E=p^2/(2m)$, the proton momentum is $p=\sqrt{2mE}=\sqrt{2(1.67\times10^{-27})(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})}=2.3117\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The $1.00\%$ uncertainty gives $\Delta p=2.3117\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum is about $h/\Delta p=2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses a momentum uncertainty far larger than the stated 1.00% when substituted into $h/\Delta p$.
perOption.B: Also implies a momentum uncertainty far larger than 1.00% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the result with the syllabus uncertainty estimate.
perOption.D: Implies a smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.00%.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: C follows the H2 syllabus estimate using h. The exact standard-deviation bound uses h/(4π), which gives about 2.28 × 10⁻¹³ m, absent from the options.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: An alpha decay moves two squares left and two down, removing two protons and two neutrons. A beta-minus decay moves one square right and one down, changing a neutron into a proton. Working backwards from Y by two beta-minus steps leads to P, so two successive beta-minus decays take P to Y.

perOption.A: Correct. Two beta-minus decays take P to Y.
perOption.B: Q needs one alpha and two beta-minus decays, for three steps.
perOption.C: R has mass number 231, which cannot fall to 228 in changes of zero or four.
perOption.D: S has mass number 235, which cannot fall to 228 in changes of zero or four.

vjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Subtract the background first to get the source count rate of $532-24=508$ counts per minute. After two half-lives, the source count rate is $508/4=127$ counts per minute. Adding back the background gives $127+24=151$ counts per minute.

perOption.A: Reports the decayed source count without restoring the background.
perOption.B: Quarters the entire initial detector reading, including the background.
perOption.C: Correct. It includes the source count after decay and the background.
perOption.D: Quarters the total initial reading and then adds the background again.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Taking the cyclist’s mass as $80\ \mathrm{kg}$ and speed as $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $E_k=\tfrac12(80)(5)^2=1000\ \mathrm J$, so B is realistic. From $v=f\lambda$, a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wave has frequency $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$. An atom with mass number 1 to 200 has a mass of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and a $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has momentum $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: The frequency is far too low, with a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wavelength giving $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
perOption.B: Correct. A cyclist can have about $1\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Atomic masses are typically of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.D: The estimate is far too high, as $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.issues: The key’s atom-mass line gives a single number for a range of mass numbers. The explanation expresses the resulting orders of magnitude as a range.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Rearrange each set of force vectors tip to tail without changing their directions or lengths. Only D gives a closed vector triangle and hence zero resultant force, as required for equilibrium. A, B and C all give a nonzero resultant.

perOption.A: Both diagonal vectors have rightward components, so the horizontal forces cannot cancel.
perOption.B: The vertical and diagonal vectors both have downward components, with no upward component to balance them.
perOption.C: All three vectors have downward components, so the vertical forces cannot cancel.
perOption.D: Correct. The three vectors form a closed triangle when arranged tip to tail.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: As the person approaches Q, their clockwise moment about Q decreases. The balancing anticlockwise moment decreases, so the downward force at P decreases. The upward force at Q balances the two weights plus the downward force at P, so it also decreases.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The upward force at Q falls as the downward force at P falls.
perOption.C: The shorter moment arm reduces the downward force required at P.
perOption.D: Both forces decrease as the person's clockwise moment decreases.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The person's weight is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on the person. Its Newton's third-law partner is the gravitational force exerted by the person on the Earth.

perOption.A: Tension acts on the person and belongs to the rope–person interaction.
perOption.B: Upthrust acts on the person and belongs to the air–person interaction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This gravitational force pairs with the helicopter's pull on the person.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: For the falling stone, use $s=ut_1+\frac{1}{2}gt_1^2$ with zero initial speed to get $t_1=3.988\ \mathrm{s}$. The sound takes $t_2=78.0/330=0.236\ \mathrm{s}$ to travel back up the well. The total is $t_1+t_2=4.224\ \mathrm{s}$, which rounds to $4.22\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the sound travel time from the fall time.
perOption.B: Counts only the fall time.
perOption.C: Uses $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which gives a shorter fall time.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The electrical input power multiplied by efficiency equals the gain in gravitational potential energy per unit time. Thus $P_\mathrm{in}=\frac{400\times9.81\times1200}{120}\div0.80=49\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Uses the efficiency factor in the wrong direction and is about a factor of ten below even that estimate.
perOption.B: Underestimates the correctly efficiency-adjusted power by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Multiplies the useful power by efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: Both coins start with the same speed and fall through the same net height. By conservation of energy, they gain the same kinetic energy per unit mass and therefore hit the ground with the same speed.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Y rises before falling, so it travels a greater vertical distance.
perOption.C: Y takes longer to reach the ground because it initially moves upwards.
perOption.D: With negligible air resistance, both coins have the same downward acceleration.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The key equates the coins’ total energies without specifying equal masses. The energy comparison applies per unit mass.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: By Newton's third law, the particles exert equal and opposite forces on each other during the collision, so their momentum changes are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Hence $4|\Delta v_X|=9|\Delta v_Y|$, giving $\left|\frac{\Delta v_X}{\Delta v_Y}\right|=\frac{9}{4}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Takes a square root as if the momentum change depended on velocity squared.
perOption.C: Equates velocity changes despite the different masses.
perOption.D: Uses an inverted square-root mass ratio instead of the inverse mass ratio.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Since $v=r\omega$ and $\omega$ is constant, the linear speed increases with radius. The centripetal acceleration $a=r\omega^2$ also increases with radius.

perOption.A: Treats linear speed as fixed and then predicts a decrease in centripetal acceleration.
perOption.B: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant linear speed.
perOption.C: Overlooks the radius factor in $a=r\omega^2$.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: Both satellites are at the same orbital radius, so they experience the same gravitational field strength and hence the same centripetal acceleration. Their gravitational forces differ because $F=mg$ and their masses differ. Their common period of about 24 hours gives the same angular velocity, so $v=r\omega$ gives the same speed, while their different masses give different kinetic energies.

perOption.A: This statement is true because $F=mg$ differs for the two masses at the same field strength.
perOption.B: Correct. Both satellites have the same centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: This statement is true because both satellites have the same orbital period.
perOption.D: This statement is true because the satellites have equal speeds and different masses.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: Q's free oscillations die away faster, so Q is more strongly damped. Its frequency-response curve lies below P's at positive driving frequencies, which rules out A and B. Q has a lower peak at a slightly lower frequency than P.

perOption.A: Shows Q above P over parts of the frequency range.
perOption.B: Shows Q crossing above P and peaking at a higher frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the more strongly damped Q a taller peak.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Zero initial transmission means the incident polarisation is perpendicular to the first filter's transmission axis. At the inserted second filter, $I_1=I_0\cos^2(90^\circ-40^\circ)=I_0\cos^2 50^\circ=0.413I_0$. At the original first filter, $I_2=I_1\cos^2 40^\circ=0.413I_0\times0.587=0.24I_0$.

perOption.A: Ignores the change in polarisation produced by the inserted filter.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $40^\circ$ for both Malus’ law factors.
perOption.D: Stops at the intensity after the inserted filter.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key’s last line labels the final intensity $I_1$ instead of $I_2$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: Since $I=kA^2$, if the amplitude from $S_2$ is $A$, the amplitude from $S_1$ is $2A$. The resultant amplitude is $2A+A=3A$ at P and $2A-A=A$ at Q. Thus $\frac{I_P}{I_Q}=\frac{(3A)^2}{A^2}=9.0$.

perOption.A: Reverses the bright-to-dark intensity ratio.
perOption.B: Adds and subtracts intensities directly, giving $5/3$.
perOption.C: Uses the source intensity ratio without combining the waves.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The key labels the resultant amplitude at Q as $A_P$ in one line.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Use $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\frac{1}{300\times1000}\sin90^\circ=n(690\times10^{-9})$, giving an order limit of about $4.83$. The highest observable integer order is $4$, so there are $4+1+4=9$ bright spots.

perOption.A: Counts the nonzero orders on only one side.
perOption.B: Omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up to five even though the fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: At the same temperature, the molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, so $\frac12 m_1c_1^2=\frac12 m_2c_2^2$. Rearranging gives $\frac{c_1}{c_2}=\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses a direct mass ratio and omits the square root.
perOption.B: Inverts the mass ratio under the square root.
perOption.C: Equates the speeds instead of the mean kinetic energies.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The narrow tube has negligible volume, and the containers have the same pressure at steady state. With gas mass $m'$ and molar mass $M$, $pV=nRT=(m'/M)RT$. Equating the pressures gives $\frac{m(300)}{2V}=\frac{m'_Y(400)}{V}$, so $m'_Y=\frac38m$.

perOption.A: This mass would make the pressure in Y lower than in X.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Accounts for the temperature ratio but omits the difference in volume.
perOption.D: Assumes equal pressures imply equal gas masses.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Heating transfers energy into the gas, so $Q>0$. The gas expands and does work on its surroundings, so the work done on the gas satisfies $W<0$. The temperature rises, increasing the ideal gas's internal energy, so $\Delta U>0$.

perOption.A: Treats heating as heat loss and expansion as compression.
perOption.B: Uses the sign for work done by the gas instead of work done on it.
perOption.C: Treats the heating as heat loss and overlooks the rise in internal energy.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: After a long time in thermal contact, the spheres reach the same temperature. At thermal equilibrium there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.

perOption.A: Total internal energy also depends on the number of particles.
perOption.B: Their different surface areas mean equal temperature alone does not ensure equal radiated power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A larger radius alone does not imply greater internal energy per atom at the same temperature.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key assumes thermal equilibrium and overstates the distractor explanations: radiated power also depends on emissivity, and equal temperature alone need not imply equal internal energy per atom for different metals.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The charge transferred by the lightning flash is $\Delta Q=It$. Since $\Delta Q=C\Delta V$, the potential difference decreases by $It/C$. For parallel plates, $E=V/h$, so the field strength decreases by $\frac{It}{Ch}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses current in place of transferred charge by omitting the flash duration.
perOption.C: Multiplies the transferred charge by capacitance and omits division by plate separation.
perOption.D: Multiplies by capacitance where finding the potential difference requires division.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The steady current dissipates power $I^2R$. The alternating current dissipates mean power $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(R/2)$. Equating the two gives $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{2}I$.

perOption.A: Halves the current along with the resistance, reducing the power.
perOption.B: Treats the steady current as the peak of the alternating current.
perOption.C: Keeps the current unchanged even though halving the resistance then halves the power.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The printed options contain radicals that are missing from the question text layer.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: For a short added length, $\Delta R\approx\rho\,\Delta x/A$, where $A$ is its cross-sectional area. As the wire thickens, each added length contributes less resistance, so the graph becomes less steep. As the wire thins, each added length contributes more resistance, so the graph steepens again.

perOption.A: Correct. The gradient falls and then rises.
perOption.B: Makes the graph steepest near the thickest part, where resistance increases most slowly.
perOption.C: Keeps flattening after the wire begins to thin.
perOption.D: Steepens throughout, missing the initial flattening as the wire thickens.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: A is the only curve with the intended gradient changes, but its sketch shows a small positive intercept where $R(0)$ should be zero. The key’s resistance formula applies locally for the varying area.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Reducing the variable resistance lowers the external equivalent resistance and increases the total current. The larger voltage drop across the internal resistance lowers the terminal potential difference $V$. The fixed resistor therefore carries less current. Since the total current rises while the fixed-branch current falls, the variable-branch current $I$ rises.

perOption.A: Assumes the variable-branch current falls with the terminal voltage, ignoring the change in current split.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Misses the increased internal voltage drop and the rise in variable-branch current.
perOption.D: Overlooks the increased voltage drop across the internal resistance.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The right and bottom resistors are in series, giving $2R$, which is in parallel with the diagonal resistor to give $2R/3$. Adding the top resistor in series gives $5R/3$. That branch is in parallel with the left resistor, giving $0.625R$ between X and Y. Thus $120=0.625R$, so $R=192\ \Omega$, which rounds to $190\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Treats the equivalent resistance as the resistance of one resistor.
perOption.B: This value gives only $93.75\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.C: This value gives only $106.25\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.D: Correct. The calculated resistance rounds to $190\ \Omega$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The vertical wire produces a magnetic field into the page on its right. The current in the horizontal wire flows right, so the magnetic force on it acts upwards. It therefore has no component towards the vertical wire.

perOption.A: Parallel currents in the same direction attract.
perOption.B: The slanted wire's upward current component produces a force towards the vertical wire.
perOption.C: Correct. The force on the horizontal wire acts upwards.
perOption.D: The antiparallel currents produce a repulsive force.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.issues: C is the intended answer because the force on the horizontal wire has no component towards or away from the vertical wire. D is also defensible as worded because antiparallel currents repel and therefore exert no attractive force.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Multiply the number of turns $N$ by the field component normal to the coil and by the coil area $A$. Since $\theta$ is the angle to the plane, this gives $N\times B\sin\theta\times A=BNA\sin\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the plane and omits the number of turns.
perOption.B: Calculates only the flux through one turn.
perOption.C: Uses $B\cos\theta$, the field component parallel to the plane.
perOption.D: Correct. It uses the normal field component and all $N$ turns.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: A photon has energy $hf$, so the emission rate is $N/t=P/(hf)=P\lambda/(hc)$. Substitution gives $(0.50\times10^{-3})(6.4\times10^{-7})/[(6.63\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)]=1.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It divides laser power by the energy per photon.
perOption.B: This rate would require about $0.81\ \mathrm{W}$ at the stated wavelength, indicating an error in the power scale.
perOption.C: Taking milli- as $10^3$ instead of $10^{-3}$ overstates the rate by a factor of $10^6$.
perOption.D: This rate implies a photon energy of about $7.8\times10^{-43}\ \mathrm{J}$, far below $hc/\lambda$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: For the minimum momentum uncertainty use $\Delta x\,\Delta p\approx h$. The slit width gives $\Delta p\approx(6.63\times10^{-34})/(1.3\times10^{-7})=5.1\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The width is vertical, so the corresponding momentum uncertainty is vertical.

perOption.A: Correct. The slit width sets the vertical momentum uncertainty.
perOption.B: Uses the direction of travel for the uncertainty even though the slit confines the electron vertically.
perOption.C: Identifies the correct direction but overestimates the uncertainty given by $h/\Delta x$.
perOption.D: Overestimates $h/\Delta x$ and assigns the uncertainty to the horizontal direction.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: There are ten tin nuclei for every remaining antimony nucleus, so the surviving fraction is $N/N_0=1/11$. Using $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/60$ per day gives $\ln(1/11)=-(\ln 2/60)t$. Thus $t=208$ days, between 180 and 240 days.

perOption.A: Stops before three half-lives, when the tin-to-antimony ratio is still below 7.
perOption.B: Stops at three half-lives, when the ratio is 7.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio reaches 10 after about 208 days.
perOption.D: Waits four half-lives, by which point the ratio is 15.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235\times7.6$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the sign of the released energy, leading to a decrease in total binding energy.
perOption.B: Carries the uranium binding energy per nucleon over to the products and fails to account for the released energy.
perOption.C: Gives a binding energy increase of only $78\ \mathrm{MeV}$, undercounting the released energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The total binding energy increases by about $195\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
